## 5. Once Upon a Time in America (1984)

**Score:** 25
**Body:** Sergio Leone's last film, with Robert De Niro and James Woods as friends from the Lower East Side. It isn't told in order: it moves between the 1920s, the 1930s and 1968, with memories and the present sliding into each other. It's nearly four hours long, so one for the weekend.

The original US theatrical release was drastically shortened and recut in chronological order, leading to an incomprehensible narrative. Leone's full vision didn't reach the viewing public until more than 20 years after his death.

If you're in the UK it's free on ITVX at the moment, and in the US it's free on Tubi.

3. Worth sustaining the opening scene of that phone ringing! One of the very first films I purchased - in the cloud. May just be James Woods' best. It's Sergio Leone. Ennio too. Epic. Also important - an Italian's perspective on CRIME in America during and directly after Prohibition. Much better, IMHO, than 'Once Upon a Time In the West.' Also a very good film, but still not as good as this one. An epic masterpiece.
4. A beautiful and melancholic tale of greed, ambition, friendship, love, loss and regret.

I'm going to have to check this out.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Lifeforce (1985)

**Score:** 47
**Body:** Lifeforce (1985)  
Rating: 10/10  
Watched: November 5, 2026



Before we even talk about the movie itself, we need to talk about Mathilda May. It's important, because looked at through the lens of progress, an 18-year-old dancer walking around completely naked for the entire duration of the movie is one hell of a hot-button issue.

It's fair to say two things: one, that the thought of being completely nude in front of God and country wasn't something she thought she'd ever be asked to do. Two, even though it was tremendously overwhelming in the beginning and there were some arguments about how she was presented, May ultimately came to appreciate the role.

Mathilda's performance as Space Girl (yes, really) is undeniably titillating. She's absolutely beautiful, and it's hard not to stare, but that was kind of Tobe Hooper's point for the movie; Space Girl is the most overwhelmingly female creature any man has ever seen, and it's one of the ways in which she turns regular people into freaky space vampires.

Well, I think of them more as freaky space vampire-zombies because when they're in their hungriest phase, they're emaciated and mad with hunger.

And it's that hunger that propels the rest of the movie. Drained of all Lifeforce from Space Girl, they themselves need to feed in the same exact manner, and every time they feed, they turn their victims into the same thing. I very much appreciate the accelerated pace here, and it shows something that not a lot of movies like this get right.

The expansion of the plague truly is exponential. I don't know the exact timeframe of the movie in terms of days, but once Space Girl drains her first victim of Lifeforce, it isn't long before the whole of London is infested. Other movies don't really address that at all, or if they do, it lacks something.

The sight of London transformed into a nightmare city full of hungering, slavering vampires, eager and starving, is really quite something to see, but between there and here, we get a truly unhinged performance from Steve Railsback.

This was the first time I'd ever seen Steve in anything, mostly because I was 13, but when I say unhinged, I mean unhinged. He's fairly driven mad by his experiences aboard the shuttle during the journey home, and when he returns on the scene, his time on-screen is split evenly between trying to help stop the plague and trying to find Space Girl. His reasons for finding her are very understandable, if a little esoteric and poorly explained, at least for me.

So while Carlsen is running around being half a lunatic, his counterpart, Peter Firth's Colonel Caine, is what I like to call "steadfast and stoic British Military Man, eh wot?" Yes, he's seeing some supremely weird and bizarre shit. Yes, Carlsen is plainly bonkers. Yes, his city is basically burning down around him. But no, he isn't about to let any of that stop him from getting the job done.

The last two things I need to talk about are Sir Patrick Stewart and the FX.

I'm enormously saddened by Patrick's passing, and so watching this movie, even though his part is brief, is not without a certain amount of sadness. But the thing I like most about Patrick is that even though he is both Jean-Luc Picard and the quintessential Professor Charles Xavier, the man loved acting. He did amazing stuff, and then he's like, "Yes please, I'd like to be in a space vampire movie where, at one point, I am channeling Space Girl during an interrogation, and yes, I would absolutely like to cut away just before I kiss another man with an open mouth, and yes, if you want to keep rolling, I'd be okay with that too, because I'm Patrick Stewart."

I can't help that last bit; it's been my personal head canon that Patrick, who had a wonderful sense of humor and a wicked side, fully committed to that kiss.

And lastly, we come to one of the key elements: the special effects.

They're spectacular. Helmed by John Dykstra, the movie has some of the most fantastic practical and visual effects in any movie I've ever seen.

The transference of Lifeforce, shown as electric-blue lightning tinged with other colors, is so vibrant and violent. The emaciated space vampires, while kind of hokey, are still great; these aren't wet, soppy vampires, these are desiccated and gross space vampires, and the dry, dusty-looking, wrinkled skin shows that better than anything.

Their massive ship, caught in Halley's Comet, is another wonder. We only get to see it for a short time, but they manage to give us the feeling that they really are in an alien spaceship 150 miles long. While it pushes a little too close to the Space Jockey ship that we see in Alien, forgiveness can be given. If you were a filmmaker and weren't, even accidentally, influenced by such a genre-defining movie, were you really making movies?

At the end of the day, Lifeforce is a hoot. It works on a lot of levels. Erotic sci-fi horror. Space vampire horror. City-ending terror. Naked ladies. Patrick Stewart kissing a guy and having a blast.

What's not to love?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. >While it pushes a little too close to the Space Jockey ship that we see in Alien, forgiveness can be given. If you were a filmmaker and weren't, even accidentally, influenced by such a genre-defining movie, were you really making movies?


Lifeforce is an adaptation of The Space Vampires by Colin  Wilson and was published in 1976. The reason both openings sequences are similar is that both the book and Alien are pulling from the same source of inspiration which is Lovecraft. 

It's a very flawed and problematic film on many levels adapted from a book that is tremendously more batshit, misogynistic, and sexist then the film. But that's not to say it isn't fun or entertaining which to me it is. I wouldn't give it a 10 though. It's an enjoyable lazy Saturday afternoon film.
2. This movie always cracks me up because I chose it as a rental when my parents were allowing me to watch rated R movies with supervision. They would often just quickly fast forward anything they didn’t want me to see, but with Lifeforce they just yanked the VHS tape out of the VCR and returned it. I don’t think I got around to seeing it until 30 years later. 🤣 
3. What a movie. This is the kind of movie that makes you exclaim that once you are done.
4. Twas the first time I saw Sir Pat in anything - but not the primary reason for watching, being 15yrs old at the time... 
Certainly a decent and enjoyable sci-fi/horror B-movie, if nothing else.
5. There's a friend of mine that, to this day, calls the movie Assforce because of Mathilda May. I think this movie caused more than a few hormonal epiphanies back in the day. But it's one of those sneak attack movies. Like, as a youth, maybe you sign up for the nudity but the movie is so bonkers and awesome in so many other aspects that it's really a pleasure to watch. 
6. What I love about this movie is that it is still Dracula, but with the sex of the vampire and the lover/victim reversed. The astronaut is under her spell; he gets hypnotized and can report where she is; he and she share true love and end up together anyway. 

The dried up victims fucked me up as a kid. So scary!

Oh— the best part is of course Patrick Stewart getting stabbed in the neck with two syringes. Or when he vomits up the blood monster. 

## 2. Thoughts about the state of film criticism with relation to box-office and creative, ambitious risks like Digger

**Score:** 29
**Body:** I wrote a piece on my Substack recently that has echoed in my mind for a minute about the state of film criticism, especially as it relates to auteur-driven risk-taking films. Films that lay it all on the line for the sake of art and expression. Films like Megalopolis, Babylon, and most recently Digger. I'm thinking the hundreds of million dollar risks that get pounced by critics who complain of their "excess" that are "doing too much". That's the general hostility and vibe I get from critics with these kind of projects.

The films I mentioned are all different films, and I'm not suggesting they're all successful. It's perfectly reasonable to dislike these movies. I've disliked ambitious auteur projects myself. But I've noticed how quickly conversations around these films become dominated by their budgets, box-office failures, and whether they were worth the financial risk. Instead of discussing what a filmmaker attempted, what worked, what failed, or what was interesting about the experience, we end up talking about how much money was lost. The films themselves almost become secondary to the spectacle of their failure. That there's a sort of glee that the critics take in a major Hollywood risk failing, as if they're parroting the tune of the top brass of Hollywood studios who don't want to fund expensive art in favor of sure-fire moneymakers.

A critic obviously isn't obligated to like a film, and I don't think filmmakers should be immune to harsh criticism just because they have an ambitious vision. But should critics have some responsibility beyond evaluating individual works? Shouldn't they also advocate for the continued existence of a film culture where filmmakers can take enormous creative risks, even when those risks don't pay off commercially? I mean on some level critics should endorse projects that fit the vision for the landscape they want to see, instead of punishing films that contribute to that. Especially, when the reaction to mediocrity is uneventful.

As I mentioned, I wrote a longer piece about this in relation to the violent responses to Digger that I felt were completely unwarranted. But, I'm genuinely curious if other people here have thought about this dynamic in modern film criticism. Please let me know your thoughts. I will also gently put my substack link if you want to read more of my thoughts:  
[https://abhinavyerramreddy.substack.com/p/why-do-critics-punish-creativity?r=38m95e&utm\_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm\_medium=post%20viewer](https://abhinavyerramreddy.substack.com/p/why-do-critics-punish-creativity?r=38m95e&utm_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm_medium=post%20viewer)

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. You thesis seems rather dubious.  Of course the media as a whole will talk about financial failures, that that is part of the job of the trade press, and it always has been.  That isn't film criticism.

I don't know it is typical of the best film critics to center "gleeful" discussions about box office failures in their analysis of films.  Indeed it would be odd if they did, because most working film critics at major publications write criticism that is published at the theatrical premiere before anyone knows the box office results.  

That the discourse on the internet as a whole makes fun of pretentious failures may be true, but the broad sentiments of the crowd aren't "film criticism" 
  - One reason that I am skeptical of thesis like this is because nine times out of ten, when I see a response to critics (or other groups that are often seen as influential and elitist), the person slinging these criticisms does not include any examples whatsoever. In a Reddit comment, that's not a big deal, but I expect a long and - hopefully researched - Substack article to name names and I did not see that. 

What I often see instead is people seeing the general criticism in the environment and attributing that to critics. Anything in the ether that they didn't like is a critic's fault even if the critic may not have been in the room. Case and point, I skimmed this Substack article and only found two examples of OP linking to an article that is supposed to be emblematic of their point. 

**- "The Digger disaster: what an epic movie flop means for Tom Cruise and Hollywood" by Catherine Shoard**. 

\- **"‘Sinners’ Is a Box Office Success (With a Big Asterisk)" by Brooke Barnes.** 

Neither of these articles are reviews by critics. They are not labeled as reviews. They did not come out when reviews typically come out (before or opening weekend of a movie). They are not written by people with Film critic or reviewers anywhere in their title, nor do their authors review films in a part-time fashion despite their titles. I don't even think they're stored in the same sections of their respective editorials. Both of them are categorized as news, more specifically business (media) news.

So now we have a substack article attacking critics that seems unable or uninterested in citing or quoting any critics at all, not actually capable of substantiating that what's being complained about is a thing that critics do at all.
    - You put into words my issue with so many “hot take” write ups like these. The reason that courts of law use facts is because “vibes” arguments can often distort reality and hinder decision making. Some call this type of argumentation “empty rhetoric” and it’s become more prevalent than ever.
      - Thanks! I noticed it in myself years ago. I would see a trend in people's behavior online after an event or discourse, think "wow, this is a real problem in [insert community]" Then I started going back and trying to actually document those instances and those "so many" videos or posts or comments went from feeling like dozens to like 5. 

Our brains try to make patterns out of phenomena to explain our world, but people are quick to make patterns without evidence. On top of that, the messiness of the Internet leads to a confusion of context. Everything gets mixed together and it's hard to keep things straight. Was it really **critics** saying negative things, did you check? How often were they negative as opposed to just lukewarm? Are you only seeing what critics say if it pops up on your feed or are you digging deep to get a holistic view of what they think? 

The more time I spend documenting social or cultural phenomena I see, the more skeptical I am of this stuff as just confirmation bias unless the person has produced examples. After all, if something really is a big problem, it should be very quick to produce examples. I even have a list of YouTube video essays that are guilty of doing the thing I'm accusing this post of doing lol.
2. Have you considered that the "risk" didn't pay off for these "risk-taking" films? Inherent to that nature is the high chance they'll fail, otherwise they wouldn't be risky. 

Other than that, I think you're mistaken viewing the culture of cinema as a manichean struggle between good vs evil: commerce vs art; auteur vs studio. All these distinctions are pretty loose, especially when auteur theory (at least in it's American form as articulated by Sarris) was based on analyzing directors deeply entrenched in the studio system (Ford, Hitchcock, Lubitch, Wilder, etc) and the auteur policy that arose in the post-war and New Hollywood era largely turned these "auteurs" into brands that were commercially lucrative.

Cinema is a personal art, in that it's often (but not always) guided by the viewpoint of a director. But it's also an industrial art, and an extremely expensive one, on par with architecture or city planning. Not only do films have to recoup their costs in order to exist, they are also collective efforts, requiring vast amounts of labor and capital to accomplish. Attributing the entirety of the effort to one man and/or endowing him with complete "creative control" can evoke a romantic notion of individual freedom... but in practice it can mean an unaccountable entrepreneurial tyrant treating his workers like slaves and mistaking the subject they work on for his own ego.
3. I don’t see much criticism around these films focusing on budget. I see a lot of people online who get a thrill out of watching a movie’s failure who focus in on that, and that becomes a very loud voice in the dialogue, but genuine criticism seems about the same as it always was. 

The examples you give were mostly criticized for not justifying their approach, despite great ambitions and risk taking. Unfortunately ambition and risk aren’t enough on their own, and these movies struggled to find a critical audience that cares about them.

## 4. Thoughrs on HAPPY TOGETHER (1997), directed by Wong Kar-Wai

**Score:** 6
**Body:** I've been seeing a lot of praise on Reddit for movies by one of my favorite filmmakers, Wong Kar-Wai, but not many for his acclaimed 1997 drama, HAPPY TOGETHER, specifically.

This prompted me to look up an essay I wrote about it, for a film class more than 20 (!) years ago.

What's fascinating is that I don't remember writing any of this, but I checked and apparently, I didn't copy it from anywhere. (That's a relief!)

I also don't remember the actual movie having last watched it so long ago, but re-reading what I'd written definitely makes me want to!


"The Heart Has Its Reasons; or, Starting Over Again With Wong Kar-Wai

The setting is Argentina, birthplace of the tango. We get to hear some of that music in the background of various scenes.

I cannot say whether the two relationships at the heart of "Happy Together" are tangos in themselves. After all, it seems like the tango can be a metaphor for anything nowadays. If it implies an irresistable attraction, which we are helpless to fight off, though we know it will lead to disaster, Lai Yiu-Fai (Tony Leung Chiu-Wai) and Ho Wo-Ping (Leslie Cheung) are definitely dancing a tango. Likewise, if it means finding comfort in the presence of a kindred spirit, Yiu-Fai and his young friend Chang (Chang Chen) are tango-bound.

Though Argentina is a sunny country, "Happy Together" is, for the most part, not a sunny picture. Lai Yiu-Fai’s relationship with Ho Wo-Ping gets the majority of screen time, but theirs is a most turbulent affair. As Yiu-Fai’s voiceover tells us, they have known each other for a long time. But within that span, they have butt heads, broken up, and gotten back together, too often to keep count. Wo-Ping is usually the one who does the dumping. He is also the one who crawls back, and asks to start the relationship over again. Yiu-Fai always takes Wo-Ping back, thus perpetuating their vicious cycle. "Happy Together" observes a stretch of their on-again/off-again relationship, which is severed by jealousy and resentment. Eventually, Wo-Ping looks to reconcile again. But this time, Yiu-Fai has had enough.

"Happy Together" might put some viewers off, because it is about gay men. But this movie has very little interest in the politics of homosexuality. It is more interested in portraying the ordeal of its main character, Lai Yiu-Fai, in a way that is true to life. His emotional struggle is meant to be universal: the unextinguished candle that still burns for the love object; the insecurity and mistrust that degenerates into possessiveness; gradually understanding that things were not meant to be.

While the movie sounds simple, writer/director Wong Kar-Wai understands that the emotions involved are deep and complex. So the way he conducts the film, he plays the emotions like a kind of music. He underscores his characters’ silent longings with French New Wave-style flair, making them big as life.

Kar-Wai uses slow-motion, freeze shots, and multi-angle edits to turn seemingly meaningless moments into intervals of great profundity. When a character places his head on another character’s shoulder, it’s shot in slow-motion, with tango playing in the background. Slow-motion draws attention to their faces; we can practically read what Lai Yiu-Fai feels—suspicion combined with genuine temptation. By using tango, Kar-Wai reminds us that his characters, though they are sitting in a cab and staring straight ahead, are engaging, emotionally, in a give-and-take that indeed qualifies as a dance. Another interesting moment occurs when Lai Yiu-Fai walks into a men’s room, and unexpectedly finds Ho Wo-Ping. The picture freezes. Lai Yui-Fai is surprised, his emotions overwhelmed. As a result, his reality, represented by the film itself, momentarily seizes up.

The director also employs an unique narrative device to give his characters’ relationship added depth. A scene will be shown, such as Yiu-Fai receiving a call from Wo-Ping, or him startling Wo-Ping and accusing him of rifling through his closets. Then the film flashes back to a prior event, which may have taken place minutes, hours, or days before. Kar-Wai and Christopher Doyle, his frequent cinematographer, elect to use black-and-white photography for the flashbacks. This way, when we see Wo-Ping, alone in his plush hotel room, go out into the hallway to call Yiu-Fai, or Wo-Ping rummaging through the closets, it doesn’t impede the story. We can tell the difference between what is happening now, and what happened in the past.

Why does the director choose to structure the film in this fashion? Why detour from chronological order? By intercutting flashbacks into the linear narrative, Kar-Wai gives us two points of view for every scene he meddles with. This way, we can observe how the characters distrust each other, how even basic interactions feature deceit. In the previous example, Yiu-Fai only knew that his personal belongings had been tossed about. Thanks to the flashbacks, we know (and Yiu-Fai doesn’t) that Wo-Ping was looking for a particular thing.

We are privy to information one character has, which the other does not have. When Yiu-Fai gets the call from Wo-Ping, and the invitation to his hotel, he assumes that Wo-Ping wants to show off the spoils of his gigolo lifestyle. Far from it. Wo-Ping has a comfortable bed, and luxuries meant to satisfy his hedonistic urges. Pornography blares from his hotel room TV. The dresser is decorated with open bottles of alcohol. What’s conspicuously missing, however, is intimacy of any sort. To try and alleviate the aching of his heart, Wo-Ping reaches out to Yiu-Fai. But Yiu-Fai is not privy to the flashbacks, nor the information they contain. As a result, he does not realize his former lover’s intent, nor the complicated emotions that inform his actions.

As a final nod to Kar-Wai’s gift for mise-en-scene, "Happy Together" might contain the boldest example of symbolism I have seen in his movies. There is a shot of a giant waterfall, used to underscore Lai Yiu-Fai’s emotional state after being dumped. The sight of the waterfall (which is presented via a slow, panning shot, probably done from a helicopter) delivers a powerful emotional impact. It is conveniently juxtaposed. It follows the scene where Wo-Ping tells him that their days together are dull. Yiu-Fai walks towards the camera, head down. He looks grief-stricken. When we see the waterfall, we infer that the thousands of gallons pouring from the falls represent the sorrow gushing forth from Yiu-Fai’s heart. It’s a picture that speaks a thousand words, from a man who really knows how to use images to encompass volumes.

"Lai-Yiu Fai… We could start over again."

These are words his lover, Ho Wo-Ping, constantly says to him. When he wants to break up, he offers that caveat. Someday, perhaps, they can start over again. Eventually, Wo-Ping will want to get back together. Then he will say the same thing: “Lai Yiu-Fai… We could start over again.”

How interesting that Wong Kar-Wai should set “Happy Together,” about two gay men who try to start a new life together, in Argentina. After all, during the 1880’s, immigrants from all over the world flocked there to begin anew. Of course, they could never leave the Old World behind completely. When time came to commiserate about failed romance or cultural alienation, these immigrants from Europe, Africa, and other distant lands drowned their sorrows in the tango. The tango combined familiar musical styles with some unfamiliar ones. It produced an exotic sound, but also reflected home.

Over a hundred years after the original immigrants, Lai Yui-Fai and Ho Wo-Ping also try to start anew. But can a person really begin again? Can we return to a past romantic partner, without digging up old resentments? Wong Kar-Wai seems to argue that you can indeed start over. But only if you are a different person than you were the previous time. Otherwise, the past has a tendency to repeat itself, as it does for Lai Yiu-Fai and Ho Wo-Ping.

Yiu-Fai and Wo-Ping face a nearly-insurmountable obstacle. Wo-Ping is selfish, indulges too much. He is too much attracted to Argentina's wild nightlife. Yiu-Fai, on the other hand, is practical, giving, and responsible. His and Wo-Ping’s values greatly differ. When they get back together in Argentina, things go well for a while. But only because Wo-Ping needs Yiu-Fai’s help. Special circumstances lead to this comfortable, symbiotic relationship developing. It only lasts, however, for as long as Wo-Ping remains hurt.

As soon as Wo-Ping’s begins recovering from his beating, he regresses to his old ways. This leads to conflict, and inevitable dissolution. Part of the problem is Wo-Ping, who is unwilling to change his behavior. But at the same time, Yiu-Fai will not stop being possessive. At one point, Yiu-Fai buys two entire cartons of cigarettes, so Wo-Ping won’t have that excuse to leave the apartment at night. This sends him into a brief rage. Wo-Ping makes it clear to Yiu-Fai, who would rather he stayed home, "If I want to go out, I’ll go out."

Jealousy and suspicion also seep in. These two know each other too well, and have experienced too much pain at the other’s hands. It must have occurred to Yiu-Fai that his partner might get bored, and leave again. So he takes something of Wo-Ping’s. This stolen object guarantees that, even if he leaves, he cannot get too far.

How much better it would be if Yiu-Fai and Wo-Ping started over alone. Especially since neither character has changed since they last broke up. For them, there is no point in trying to start again. If their personality conflicts drove them apart in the past, and both men are still the same, history must repeat itself. Of course, if their relationship did not collapse again, Wong Kar-Wai would not have his movie. One of the truths about the human heart, which “Happy Together” espouses very well, is that sometimes, the mighty organ cannot help itself. It yearns for the departed. It tosses aside common sense to try and reclaim some joy from the past.

But the heart can also find pleasure in something new. One day, Yiu-Fai crosses paths with Chang, who works at the restaurant where Yiu-Fai has taken a job. Gradually, they get to know each other. We can tell from his voiceovers that Chang is a sensitive boy.

Yiu-Fai relates to Chang much differently than with Wo-Ping. With the latter, the attraction was mostly physical, and Kar-Wai established this early on. The very first shot of the movie showed Yiu-Fai’s naked body being observed by Wo-Ping. He followed that up with a scene of them having sex. By contrast, Yiu-Fai and Chang share a deeper, more emotional bond. Both their souls are homesick. Chang, however, wants to see more of the world before going back.

Although their relationship never becomes sexual, Chang gives Yiu-Fai something more important: Strength to truly start over fresh. Hearing Chang talk about home, and his family, he is reminded of a past indiscretion. He realizes that he cannot go home as the same person, for the injured party will not accept him. So Yiu-Fai begins the process of change by writing a long letter to the injured. Once upon a time, he could not imagine doing such a thing. Yet here he is, writing the letter. But Yiu-Fai still isn’t ready to return home. He must embark on a descent into the underworld, where he wanders aimlessly through Argentina’s gay subculture. It is an abyss of orange sunsets and temptations of the flesh.

With Chang gone, and Wo-Ping at a distance, Yiu-Fai finally gets the chance to stare into the abyss, and not look away. He gets an opportunity to build character. Now, when he returns home to Hong Kong, having survived loss, loneliness, and the quietus that is a solitary mind, he will be a different man. He will have conquered himself; he will have left Wo-Ping behind for good. Now he gets his chance at redemption and forgiveness. Now he can really start over."

But I was thinking about how he never won a best directing Oscar. It seems crazy considering his legacy but is it really that crazy.

He was nominated for the award 5 times 

1941 - Nominated for Rebecca but lost to John Fords  Grapes of Wrath

Rebecca is one of my favourite Hitchcock films (but still might not make the top 10, that’s how good he was) and it’s probably one of his most Oscar bait type of film, but can we really say he deserved the Oscar over John Ford. Grapes of Wrath is a classic and considered a masterclass in direction and helped forge a new path on what thought possible at the time.

1945 - Nominated for Lifeboat and lost to Leo McCarey Going My Way

I would argue that Lifeboat is the nomination he deserved the least, but the movie he lost to was nothing special either. But Double Indemnity and Laura were both nominated that year and both would have been a far better pick than Going My Way or Lifeboat

1946 - Nominated for Spellbound lost to Billy Wilder The Lost Weekend

What can you say Spellbound is a great movie and has some outstanding cinematography, but The Lost Weekend is one of the greatest Film Noirs of all time and the first film to win the Palme D’or and Best Picture in the same year.

1955 - Nominated for Rear Window lost to Elia Kazan On the Waterfront.

Once again both classic movies and both worthy of the award, but it’s not like I can’t understand why Elia won over Hitchcock

1961 - Nominated for Psycho lost to Billy Wilders The Apartment 

This is probably the only one you could really argue he got screwed, but I have a soft spot for the Apartment and consider on of the best romantic comedies of all time.

Anyway, I guess what I’m saying in the years he did get nominated it’s understandable that he lost but is there any other year you think he should have been nominated and won.

I think he should have been nominated and won for Vertigo over Vincente Minnelli and Gigi.

What do you think?

Extra hot take: My favourite Hitchcock film is Suspicion, but even that year I would give it to Orson Welles for Citizen Kane.
